newsitem.title: USA: U.S. scales back mission to help Rwanda refugees.
newsitem.headline: U.S. scales back mission to help Rwanda refugees.

text.p: The United States on Tuesday put off plans to send combat troops to Zaire and prepared instead for a military air relief operation into Rwanda to help a half-million refugees there, the Pentagon said.

Defence Secretary William Perry said the return of some 500,000 people from Zaire to Rwanda had changed the situation and that fewer than 1,000 U.S. "logistical" personnel were now needed for a military operation in Rwanda led by Canada.

Under the new plan about 200 U.S. Air Force personnel would be sent to Kigali airport in Rwanda, 500 to Entebbe in Uganda and about 100 to Mombasa in Kenya to prepare for the air relief operation, the Pentagon said.

Canada, which is leading the multinational military effort to ease the plight of the Rwandan refugees, on Tuesday put the international military relief operation on hold pending meetings this week with other countries involved.

The Pentagon stressed that President Bill Clinton, while agreeing U.S. participation in principle, has still not given final approval for the actual mission, which could change in response to circumstances on the ground.
A senior administration official termed the situation "very fluid" and said by Wednesday some 600,000 people would have returned to Rwanda from Zaire.
A final decision on the shape of the assistance effort should be taken by early next week, the official said, adding, "Obviously we need the consent of the Rwandan government."
Relief agencies were able to care for the refugees for the moment as they had adequate stocks of food and other supplies, the official said. "There is no food shortage," he said.

Pentagon spokesman Ken Bacon told reporters the U.S. Air Force had about 30 big military cargo planes waiting in Europe to carry such equipment as communications and forklift trucks to Kigali, Entebbe and Mombasa to facilitate relief operation.

Both the Pentagon and State Department stressed that several hundred thousand Rwandan refugees were still in eastern Zaire and Washington remained ready to send protective troops to Zaire in any multinational military force if needed.

"There have been more than 500,000 refugees that have peacefully returned to Rwanda in the last few days. This is a very positive development and we are modifying our plans based on this dramatic change," Perry told reporters.

"The approach that we are taking is designed to help those that have returned while at the same time leaving the multinational force prepared to help inside Zaire if that were to become necessary," Perry told reporters.

"These actions allow us to provide assistance to the repatriation effort in Rwanda pending completion of the details of this multinational force. But these actions also provide the basis for a larger mission, should that become necessary."

Bacon said a decision on the final shape of the multinational mission was expected after a meeting of U.S., Canadian and other officials in Stuttgart, Germany, planned for Thursday. U.S. officials said this may slip to Friday.
The administration official said additional meetings were scheduled in Geneva, Switzerland and New York, and the consultations would continue at least until Saturday.
Bacon said U.S. military personnel sent to Rwanda would not help distribute food, would not provide security around refugee encampments there and would not "police" such camps.
Clinton last week tentatively authorised the movement of some 1,000 armed troops into Goma, Zaire, to secure the airport and establish a corridor for the return of refugees.
But the sudden flood of refugees home beginning last Friday changed the need for protection and shifted the focus of the Canadian-led effort to Rwanda, Perry said.

"This force will require considerably fewer troops than originally envisioned and will operate chiefly in Rwanda," Perry said. "Our current thinking is that U.S. contribution to this effort will be less than a thousand troops. And these will be support logistics troops rather than combat troops."

Assistant Secretary of State George Moose said Washington was concerned that some 400,000 to 500,000 Rwandan refugees remained in Zaire south of Goma on the west side of Lake Kivu and that little was known about their numbers or whereabouts.

"We think it would be premature at best ... for us to stand down at this stage. We need to continue that planning effort and that effort is going forward," Moose said of any possible military security operation inside Zaire.
